lead: On a modern chip the metal wires between gates are often slower than the gates themselves. A wire has resistance along its length, capacitance to the layers below and to its neighbours, and inductance when the current loop is large. These are the interconnect parameters. An electrical wire model turns them into a circuit you can analyse: a lumped capacitor, a lumped RC, a distributed RC line or a transmission line, chosen by how long the wire is and how fast its edges are. This chapter shows how to compute R and C from the geometry and when each model is good enough.
prereq: You need: the RC delay estimate in switching characteristics; the metal layers come from Lithography, etching and deposition.

blocks.text: A wire of length L, width W and thickness t, made of a metal of resistivity ρ, has R = ρL/(Wt). Every metal layer has a fixed thickness, so designers fold ρ and t into one number, the sheet resistance R<sub>□</sub> = ρ/t in ohms per square. Then R = R<sub>□</sub> × (L/W): count how many W × W squares fit along the wire and multiply.

blocks.where: R<sub>□</sub> is in Ω/□; L/W is the number of squares. A square of any size has the same resistance.

blocks.text: Copper replaced aluminium in the late 1990s because its bulk resistivity is about 1.7 µΩ·cm against about 2.7 µΩ·cm. In very narrow lines electrons scatter off the surfaces and grain boundaries, so the effective resistivity is higher than the bulk value. Polysilicon and diffusion have sheet resistances hundreds of times larger than metal, so they are used only for short runs.

A wire over a ground layer is a parallel-plate capacitor: C<sub>pp</sub> = εWL/h, where h is the dielectric thickness and ε = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub> (ε<sub>r</sub> = 3.9 for silicon dioxide, ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m). In a nanometre process W is about as small as h, so field lines also leave the sides of the wire. This fringing capacitance can be larger than the plate term.

Neighbouring wires on the same layer add coupling capacitance C<sub>c</sub>. If a neighbour switches the opposite way, the voltage across C<sub>c</sub> changes by twice the swing and it acts like 2C<sub>c</sub> (the Miller factor); switching the same way it acts like zero. Coupling also injects crosstalk noise into a quiet wire. A wire's total capacitance is roughly 0.2 fF per micrometre of length, nearly independent of its width.
Cw = Cpp + Cfringe + Cc Here each term is in farads and scales with the wire length L.

Inductance. A wire and its return path form a loop with inductance. It matters only when the wire's resistance is low (wide clock and power wires) and the edges are fast compared with the time of flight, about when the rise time is under 2.5 times the flight time. Signals in silicon dioxide travel at c/√3.9 ≈ 1.5 × 10⁸ m/s, so 5 mm takes about 33 ps. Ordinary signal wires have enough resistance to damp the ringing, so RC models are used for them.

In the distributed RC line every small piece of resistance r dx drives all the capacitance after it, and the voltage obeys a diffusion equation. Its 50% step delay is 0.38RC instead of the lumped 0.69RC, where R = rL and C = cL. Both grow with L², so doubling a wire's length quadruples its own delay. Long wires are therefore broken by repeaters (buffers), which make the delay grow only linearly with length.
A π model splits the line into C<sub>w</sub>/2, R<sub>w</sub>, C<sub>w</sub>/2; a few π sections in series match the distributed line well and are what extraction tools hand to the simulator.

examples.question: A copper wire on an intermediate metal layer is L = 1 mm long, W = 0.2 µm wide and t = 0.4 µm thick, with an effective resistivity of 2.2 µΩ·cm. It sits h = 0.3 µm above the layer below, in silicon dioxide (ε<sub>r</sub> = 3.9). A field solver gives fringe capacitance 0.04 fF/µm per edge and coupling 0.05 fF/µm to each of its two neighbours. Find R<sub>□</sub>, R<sub>w</sub>, C<sub>pp</sub> and C<sub>w</sub> (neighbours quiet).
steps: Fringe: 2 edges × 0.04 fF/µm × 1000 µm = 80 fF. Coupling: 2 neighbours × 0.05 fF/µm × 1000 µm = 100 fF.
C<sub>w</sub> = 23.0 + 80 + 100 = 203 fF, that is 0.20 fF/µm. The plate term is only 11% of it.
If both neighbours switch the opposite way, the coupling counts double: C<sub>w</sub> = 23 + 80 + 200 = 303 fF.
examples.answer: R<sub>□</sub> = 0.055 Ω/□, R<sub>w</sub> = 275 Ω, C<sub>pp</sub> = 23 fF and C<sub>w</sub> ≈ 203 fF (303 fF with both neighbours switching against it).

examples.question: The inverter of the switching-characteristics chapter (R<sub>d</sub> ≈ 8.0 kΩ) drives this wire with no other load. Find the delay for L = 1 mm and L = 5 mm using the distributed RC model, and the error of the lumped RC model for the wire itself at 5 mm.
steps: 1 mm: driver term 0.69 × 8.0 kΩ × 203 fF = 1.12 ns; wire term 0.38 × 275 Ω × 203 fF = 0.021 ns. Total ≈ 1.14 ns: the wire acts as a pure capacitor (lumped C is fine).
5 mm: R<sub>w</sub> = 1375 Ω and C<sub>w</sub> = 1.015 pF. Driver term 0.69 × 8.0 kΩ × 1.015 pF = 5.60 ns; wire term 0.38 × 1375 × 1.015 pF = 0.53 ns. Total ≈ 6.13 ns.
Lumped RC for the wire alone: 0.69 × 1375 × 1.015 pF = 0.96 ns, 82% more than the distributed 0.53 ns.
The wire term grew 25 times for 5 times the length (0.021 → 0.53 ns), the L² law.
examples.answer: About 1.14 ns at 1 mm and 6.13 ns at 5 mm; the wire's own delay rises from 21 ps to 0.53 ns, and the lumped model overstates it by 82%.

traps: Using L × W instead of L/W for squares. Resistance grows with length and falls with width.
Keeping only the parallel-plate term. Fringe and coupling dominate in narrow wires.
Using 0.69RC for a distributed line. Its 50% delay is 0.38RC; 0.69RC is the lumped value.
Forgetting that wire delay grows with L², so halving the length quarters it.
Calling inductance negligible for every wire. Wide clock and power wires with fast edges need an RLC model.

quiz.q: Define sheet resistance and give its unit.
quiz.a: R<sub>□</sub> = ρ/t, the resistance of one square of a layer of thickness t, in ohms per square.

quiz.q: Why does a wire's capacitance per unit length hardly change when it is made wider?
quiz.a: A wider wire adds plate capacitance but moves away from its neighbours, so the coupling falls; fringe is set by the edges. In a dense layer the sum stays near 0.2 fF/µm.

quiz.q: A polysilicon line has R<sub>□</sub> = 8 Ω/□, W = 0.1 µm and L = 20 µm. Find its resistance.
quiz.a: 200 squares × 8 Ω = 1.6 kΩ, as much as a small transistor; poly is used only for short runs.

quiz.q: A distributed line has r = 0.3 Ω/µm and c = 0.2 fF/µm. Find its own 50% delay for L = 2 mm.
What is the Miller factor in coupling capacitance?
quiz.a: A neighbour switching the opposite way doubles the voltage change across C<sub>c</sub>, so it acts as 2C<sub>c</sub>; switching the same way it acts as 0.

quiz.q: A 10 mm wire has a delay of 2 ns on its own. Estimate the delay if it is cut into two 5 mm halves with an ideal repeater between them, and explain the result.
quiz.a: Each half has a quarter of the RC, so 0.5 ns, and two halves give 1 ns plus the repeater delay. Wire delay grows as L², so splitting it makes the total grow linearly with length.

quiz.q: When does a wire need an RLC transmission-line model rather than an RC model?
quiz.a: When its resistance is low enough not to damp ringing, as in wide clock and power wires, and its edges are faster than about 2.5 times the time of flight along it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Below about 20 nm, copper resistivity rises steeply because the barrier layer takes up much of the line, and cobalt is already used in the lowest layers while ruthenium is being studied. Low-k dielectrics and air gaps reduce capacitance. Extraction tools such as StarRC and Quantus compute R and C for every net from the layout. Search next for interconnect scaling, low-k dielectric and repeater insertion.
